descriptor.note: Copied by a script from the hub's local copy of the curriculum on 15 November 2026, not typed from memory. The VCAA site was offline that day, so the wording has not been checked against the live site. This is the Version 2.0 description behind the enduring understanding in the school's Year 3/4 concept planner Forces at Work, which quotes the earlier curriculum.
descriptor.text: forces, including frictional, gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic, can be exerted by one object on another through direct contact or from a distance and affect the motion (speed and direction) of objects
descriptor.attribution: Victorian Curriculum Foundation to Level 10 content is © VCAA, licensed CC BY-NC 3.0 Australia. The official curriculum is on the VCAA website.

paraphrase.note: My reading of the description and its achievement standard. The achievement standard wording was checked in the local copy: students identify forces acting on objects and describe the effects of these.
paraphrase.text: A force is a push or a pull that one object puts on another. Some forces need touching (friction) and some work across a gap (gravity, magnetic and electrostatic forces). Whatever the kind, a force shows itself by changing motion: it starts or stops something, speeds it up, slows it down or turns it. The assessable skills are naming the forces acting on an object and describing what they do to it.
asks_for: Forces act between two objects: one object exerts a force on another.
Some forces act through direct contact. Friction is the named example.
Some forces act from a distance: gravitational, magnetic and electrostatic forces.
Forces change motion, meaning speed and direction.
not_asking: Balanced and unbalanced forces, or how mass changes the effect of a force. Those are Levels 7 and 8 (VC2S8U14).
Measuring force in newtons, or weight against mass.
Why magnets or static charges work (fields, poles in depth, electrons). Students observe what the forces do.
Simple machines. Those are Levels 7 and 8 (VC2S8U13).

key_questions.note: My judgement. The first three questions follow the three key questions in the school's Year 3/4 concept planner Forces at Work, so the fact sheet lines up with what classroom teachers plan from. The point about moving things comes from the research summaries.
key_questions.question: What is a force, and what can it do to the way something moves?
know: A force is a push or a pull.
A force is exerted by one object on another object.
Motion means how fast something is going (speed) and which way (direction).
understand: Forces change motion: they start it, stop it, speed it up, slow it down or change its direction.
An object does not carry a force around inside it. A moving thing slows down because a force acts on it, not because its push has run out.
do: Name the two objects involved in a push or pull, and say what happened to the motion.

key_questions.note: My judgement. Shoe soles, slowing and stopping, and the positive and negative effects of friction are in a VCAA elaboration.
key_questions.question: How does friction change the motion of objects?
know: Friction is a force between two surfaces that are touching.
Friction acts against sliding. Rough surfaces usually give more friction than smooth ones.
understand: Friction slows moving things down, and it also stops things from starting to slide.
Friction is useful as well as a nuisance: it lets shoes grip, tyres hold the road and brakes work.
do: Run a fair test of how far an object travels over different surfaces, measure the distances and explain the pattern using friction.

key_questions.note: My judgement. Magnets acting without touching, gravity acting whether or not an object is moving, and astronauts on the Moon are in VCAA elaborations.
key_questions.question: Which forces can act without touching?
know: Gravitational, magnetic and electrostatic forces act from a distance.
Gravity pulls everything towards the centre of Earth, all the time, whether it is moving or still.
Magnets pull some metals, and pull or push other magnets. A rubbed balloon pulls light things towards it.
understand: Forces from a distance are still pushes and pulls. They change motion in the same way contact forces do.
These forces get weaker as the objects get further apart.
do: Predict and test what a magnet or a rubbed balloon will do to an object across a gap, and how the gap changes the result.

key_questions.note: My judgement. Force arrows showing direction and size are in a VCAA elaboration. The identifying skill is the achievement standard.
key_questions.question: How can we show the forces acting on an object?
know: A force arrow shows a force. It points the way the force acts, and a longer arrow means a bigger force.
understand: More than one force usually acts on an object at once, for example gravity down and friction against the slide.
do: Draw and label force arrows on a picture of a familiar situation, such as a ball rolling to a stop.

vocabulary.note: The choice of words and tiers is my judgement. Words marked as in the description were checked against the wording in the local copy. Exert and electrostatic are the hard words in the description and need explicit teaching.

academic.meaning: To put a force on something.
The way something is moving or pointing.
The outside or top of something.

science.meaning: A push or a pull that one object puts on another.
Movement: its speed and its direction.
The force between touching surfaces that acts against sliding.
The force that pulls objects towards the centre of Earth.
The push or pull of a magnet.
The pull or push of an object that has been charged, for example by rubbing.
To pull towards and to push away.
A force that needs touching, and a force that acts across a gap.
An arrow that shows the direction and size of a force.

misconceptions.note: Checked against the Research-2-Practice Friction summary (citing Heywood and Parker, 2001) and the IOPSpark review. Most of the studies IOPSpark names were with secondary students. Twigger et al. interviewed students aged 10 to 15. I did not read the studies.
misconceptions.idea: A moving object has a force inside it that keeps it going. It stops when the force runs out.
misconceptions.science: A moving object keeps moving until a force changes its motion. A rolling ball stops because friction acts on it.
misconceptions.respond: Roll the same ball over carpet, the desk and a smooth floor. Ask why it went further each time if the push was the same.

misconceptions.note: Checked against the IOPSpark review, which also reports the linked idea that friction always hinders motion. I did not read the studies it names.
misconceptions.idea: Friction only happens when something is moving, and it always gets in the way.
misconceptions.science: Friction also acts on things that are still: it is what stops a book sliding off a tilted desk. It helps as well as hinders, by letting shoes and tyres grip.
misconceptions.respond: Tilt a board slowly with a block on it and ask what is holding the block. Then ask what walking would be like with no friction.

misconceptions.note: Checked against the IOPSpark review, which lists a teaching resource for ages 5 to 11. The studies it names were with secondary and university students. I did not read them.
misconceptions.idea: Heavier things fall faster than lighter things.
misconceptions.science: Objects of the same shape and size fall together even when one is much heavier. Light, spread-out things such as paper fall slowly because of the air.
misconceptions.respond: Predict first, then drop two balls of the same size and different weight together. Then drop a flat sheet of paper and a scrunched one.

misconceptions.note: Checked against the IOPSpark review. The studies it names were with secondary students. I did not read them. It matters here because a VCAA elaboration uses video of astronauts on the Moon.
misconceptions.idea: Gravity needs air, so there is no gravity on the Moon or in space.
misconceptions.science: Gravity does not depend on air. The Moon has gravity, weaker than Earth's, which is why astronauts and dropped objects still come down.
misconceptions.respond: Watch astronauts drop objects on the Moon and ask what pulled them down where there is no air.

misconceptions.note: Checked against the IOPSpark review and the Research-2-Practice Magnets summary. The summary reports Bailey et al. (1987): of 119 pupils in Years 3, 5 and 7, 60 per cent predicted a larger magnet would hold more paper clips. I did not read the study.
misconceptions.idea: Magnets attract all metals, and a bigger magnet is always a stronger one.
misconceptions.science: Magnets attract only some metals: iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Size does not decide strength. A small magnet can be stronger than a large one.
misconceptions.respond: Test a set of metal objects that includes aluminium foil, a brass key and copper wire. Then count the paper clips a large and a small magnet each hold.

misconceptions.note: Checked against the IOPSpark review. The studies it names were mostly with older students and adults, so how common this is in Years 3 and 4 is not confirmed. I did not read them.
misconceptions.idea: Static electricity and magnetism are the same thing. A rubbed balloon is a kind of magnet.
misconceptions.science: They are different forces. A rubbed balloon pulls paper and hair, which a magnet does not, and a magnet pulls steel without any rubbing.
misconceptions.respond: Try the magnet and the rubbed balloon on the same set of objects (paper scraps, a steel paper clip, hair) and compare the two lists.

misconceptions.note: The science is from a VCAA elaboration (gravity acts on an object whether or not it is moving). That students think otherwise is my judgement. I did not check it against a study.
misconceptions.idea: Gravity only acts on things that are falling. Nothing is pulling on a book that is sitting on the desk.
misconceptions.science: Gravity pulls on every object all the time, moving or still. The desk holds the book up against it.
misconceptions.respond: Hold a heavy book on an outstretched hand and ask whether gravity has stopped. Then take the hand away.

inquiry.note: A VCAA elaboration for this code has students pose questions about the distance between magnets and how they attract or repel.
inquiry.how: Students ask and predict: how close does the magnet need to be before the paper clip moves? Which surface will stop the car first?

inquiry.note: Two VCAA elaborations for this code use forces: planning what to change and what to keep the same when testing which shoe has the most friction, and predicting the forces in a game or toy design, then building and testing a prototype.
inquiry.how: Students use a planning scaffold for a friction test: change the surface, keep the object, the ramp and the release the same.

inquiry.note: The code and its wording were checked in the local copy. I did not check its elaborations for a forces example, so the link is my judgement.
inquiry.skill: Planning and conducting: measuring and recording
inquiry.how: Students measure how far an object travels in centimetres with a ruler or tape, and repeat each test.

inquiry.note: A VCAA elaboration for this code has students construct a table comparing the measured distances an object moves over surfaces with different frictional forces.
inquiry.how: Students put their distances in a table or column graph and describe the pattern between surface and distance.

inquiry.note: A VCAA elaboration for this code has students make an advertisement explaining why a high-friction surface suits flooring.
inquiry.how: Students explain a choice to an audience using the science words, for example why one surface is the safest for a ramp or a floor.

human_endeavour.note: The VCAA lists this as an elaboration of VC2S4U10 itself, and names both games and the peoples and places. I did not check the detail against a Koorie or Torres Strait Islander source. Use a named source or the school's Koorie education contacts for how the games are played and what is appropriate to share.
human_endeavour.hook: Forces in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' traditional toys and games: marngrook, played in western Victoria, where a ball made from possum fur drops under gravity and is kicked high by a contact force, and kokan, played by the Mabuiag People, where sand's friction slows a ball hit with a bat.

human_endeavour.note: Both examples are VCAA elaborations for this code.
human_endeavour.hook: People use what they know about forces to solve problems: friction to make cars and bikes safer on wet or icy roads, and magnetic force to sort metals in recycling, mining and food processing.

human_endeavour.note: The VCAA lists this as an elaboration of VC2S4U10 itself.
human_endeavour.hook: Astronauts walking and dropping objects on the Moon: video evidence of gravity at work somewhere other than Earth.

below.note: The description itself names pushes and pulls as forces with strength and direction.
below.label: Pushes and pulls
below.summary: Pushes and pulls are forces that change an object's movement or shape, and have a strength and a direction. The idea this description builds on: check it first.

below.note: The code and its wording were checked in the local copy. The link is my judgement.
below.label: How objects move
below.summary: The way objects move depends on their size, shape and material. Students arrive having rolled, slid and bounced things. This description adds the forces that explain what they saw.

below.note: The code and its wording were checked in the local copy. The link is my judgement.
below.label: Technologies and movement
below.summary: Design and Technologies: how technologies make things move in products and systems. The design partner of pushes and pulls.

same.note: The description itself names forces. Its elaborations include how surfaces change the speed of a rolling marble, and First Nations examples: buoyant forces in bark and dugout canoes, and woomera design.
same.label: Forces in products
same.summary: Design and Technologies: how forces affect the way a product or system works. The hub's STEAM pairing for this description, and the pairing in Think Like an Engineer.

same.note: The code and its wording were checked in the local copy. No Digital Technologies elaboration at this level mentions forces, so this is my judgement and a loose link.
same.label: Data with software
same.summary: Digital Technologies: collecting, organising and presenting data with software. It fits when students enter their friction test distances in a spreadsheet and graph them.

above.summary: There is no Physical sciences description about forces at Levels 5 and 6. Forces appear there only as gravity in Earth and space sciences (VC2S6U07), then return in full at Levels 7 and 8. Year 3/4 is the main planned teaching of friction, magnets and static electricity in primary school.

above.note: The description itself names the force of gravity.
above.label: Gravity and orbits
above.summary: Earth and space sciences: the force of gravity keeps Earth and the other planets in orbit around the Sun. Gravity as a force from a distance, on a much bigger scale.

above.note: The description itself names balanced and unbalanced forces, gravitational force and force diagrams.
above.label: Balanced and unbalanced
above.summary: Balanced and unbalanced forces shown with force diagrams, and how an object's mass and the size and direction of forces change its motion. The direct next step, with force arrows becoming force diagrams.

above.note: The description itself says simple machines alter the direction and magnitude of forces.
above.label: Simple machines
above.summary: Levers, ramps, wedges, pulleys, screws and wheels and axles change the direction and size of forces.

above.note: The description itself names force and motion.
above.label: Force, motion, energy
above.summary: Design and Technologies: how force, motion and energy are used to control engineered systems.

above.label: Newton's laws
above.summary: Newton's laws of motion, used to analyse force, mass and acceleration with numbers.

anchors.note: Comparing measured distances over surfaces with different friction is in a VCAA elaboration for VC2S4I04. The lesson shape is my suggestion and has not been trialled. LEGO bricks are on the STEAM room inventory.
anchors.title: How far does it roll?
anchors.phenomenon: The same LEGO car released from the same ramp rolls a long way over a smooth desk, less over card and stops quickly on carpet or a towel.
anchors.students_do: Predict the order, plan a fair test with a scaffold, release the car three times on each surface, measure each distance in centimetres and put the results in a table. Explain the pattern using friction and add force arrows to a drawing of the car.
materials: A small wheeled car built from LEGO, or a marble, for each group
A ramp made from a book and a stiff board or folder
Three or four surfaces: desk, card, baking paper, a towel or carpet
anchors.shows: Gravity pulls the car down the ramp and friction slows it. Different surfaces exert different amounts of friction, which changes how far the car goes.
anchors.caution: Release, do not push. A push changes two things at once and hands students the idea that the car carries a force that runs out.

anchors.note: A magnet pulling an object without touching it is in a VCAA elaboration, and asking about the distance between magnets is in another. The lesson shape is my suggestion, not trialled. Magnets are on the STEAM room inventory. I did not check how many or what kinds.
anchors.title: The floating paper clip
anchors.phenomenon: A paper clip tied to a thread and taped to the desk stands up and strains towards a magnet held above it, with a clear gap between them. Slide card, foil or a hand through the gap and it stays up.
anchors.students_do: Find the biggest gap that still holds the clip up and measure it. Predict and test what can pass through the gap. Then test which metal objects the magnet pulls and which it ignores.
materials: A steel paper clip, thread and tape
Thin things to pass through the gap: paper, card, foil
Metal objects to test, including some a magnet does not attract: aluminium foil, a brass key, a copper coin
anchors.shows: A magnetic force acts from a distance, changes the clip's motion, and gets weaker as the gap grows. Not all metals are attracted.
anchors.caution: Keep magnets away from iPads, bank cards and anyone with a medical implant. Strong magnets can pinch fingers.

anchors.note: My suggestion, not trialled. Electrostatic force is named in the description but has no VCAA elaboration of its own. Balloons are on the STEAM room inventory.
anchors.title: The balloon and the can
anchors.phenomenon: A balloon rubbed on hair or a jumper pulls an empty drink can along the desk without touching it. Move the balloon to the other side and the can rolls back.
anchors.students_do: Predict, then race a can along the desk using only a rubbed balloon. Try the same balloon on paper scraps, a steel paper clip and a thin stream of water, and compare with what the magnet did.
materials: The magnet and test objects from the paper clip lesson, to compare
anchors.shows: An electrostatic force acts from a distance and changes the can's speed and direction. It is a different force from magnetism.
anchors.caution: It works poorly on humid days, so test it that morning. Check for latex allergies before using balloons.

pitfalls.note: The Research-2-Practice Friction summary warns about activity for its own sake in this topic and reports Wilcox et al. (2019): Year 4 pupils said they had learned how to make a bridge or a good parachute, not the science, because finishing the activity had become the point. The link to the hub's design challenges is mine.
pitfalls.pitfall: Letting the build become the lesson. In a design challenge, students can finish a boat, car or helicopter and never name a force.
pitfalls.instead: Plan one explicit question that ties the challenge to the science, such as which force slowed it down and what exerted it, and ask it before and after testing.

pitfalls.note: My judgement about teacher language. The student idea it feeds is reported in the sources.
pitfalls.pitfall: Saying that a moving object runs out of push or uses up its force.
pitfalls.instead: Name the force that changed the motion and the object that exerted it: the carpet's friction slowed the car.

pitfalls.note: My judgement, from the wording of the description, which puts contact and distance and the effect on motion ahead of the list of names.
pitfalls.pitfall: Teaching the four named forces as a list to memorise.
pitfalls.instead: Keep returning to the same three questions: what exerted the force, was it touching, and what did it do to the motion?

pitfalls.note: The positive and negative effects of friction are in a VCAA elaboration. That teaching tends to show only the negative side is my judgement.
pitfalls.pitfall: Presenting friction only as the thing that slows objects down.
pitfalls.instead: Include grip: shoe soles, tyres, brakes, and what holding a pencil would be like without friction.

pitfalls.note: My judgement, from comparing this description with VC2S8U14 and VC2S10U17 in the local copy.
pitfalls.pitfall: Reaching for balanced and unbalanced forces, newtons, or mass against weight to explain results.
pitfalls.instead: Stay with naming the forces and describing the change in speed or direction. Force arrows are enough. The rest is Levels 7 and 8.

unverified: The VCAA site was offline on 15 November 2026, so the official wording, the elaborations and the neighbouring codes were all taken from the hub's local copy of the curriculum, not from the live site. Check the description against the VCAA site when it is back.

I could not read the original research studies. Each verified misconception rests on a published summary that I read and that names the studies. Most of the studies on force, falling and gravity were with secondary students or older (the notes say which), so how common each idea is in Years 3 and 4 is not confirmed.
The last misconception (gravity only acts on falling things) is my judgement. I did not check it against a study.
The marngrook and kokan examples are confirmed only as far as the VCAA's one-sentence elaboration. I did not find or check a Koorie or Torres Strait Islander source.
None of the three anchor experiences has been trialled. I did not check how many magnets the STEAM room has or what kinds, and the balloon and can depends on a dry day.

I read only the first part of the school's concept planner Forces at Work (the curriculum links, enduring understanding and key questions), to match the description and line up the key questions. It quotes the earlier curriculum, and nothing else in it was used or checked.
The lines on the map are my judgement about how the descriptions connect. The Digital Technologies link is a loose one with no elaboration behind it.
